prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new bar. He needs to determine how profitable the company will be and convince his primary investor, his father, that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider and investigate?

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on food per visit?
What does the average customer spend on drinks per visit?
What are the labor needs and costs?
clarifying_info.a: Kitchen (when open): 4 people at $10/hr; Bar: 1 person at $5/hr; Wait staff: 3 people at $5/hr
Food has a 12% gross margin; Drinks have a 50% gross margin
No specific data on utilities, legal, insurance, licenses, training, remodeling, equipment, and other startup costs

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does the bar see?
clarifying_info.a: [Give Exhibit 1 — customer volume by day-part and day of week]

exhibits.title: Market Research — Customer Volume by Hour and Day
exhibits.shows: A table showing the number of food customers per hour and drinks customers per hour, split by two time periods (12pm–8pm and 8pm–12am/2am) and two day-of-week groups (Sunday–Wednesday vs. Thursday–Saturday)

framework: Revenue: price per customer x volume (food vs. drinks, weekday vs. weekend, day vs. night)
Labor costs: kitchen, bar, wait staff hours across operating schedule
Fixed costs: lease ($10K/month); note other unquantified costs (utilities, marketing, licenses, equipment)
Profitability: weekly/annual profit = Revenue - COGS - Labor - Lease
Investment analysis: break-even period and ROI on $500K startup capital vs. alternative investments

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly orders for food and drinks using Exhibit 1
questions.guidance: Candidate should split into Sun–Wed and Thu–Sat blocks, then day vs. night hours. Sun–Wed (4 days): day food = 10 x 8 = 80, day drinks = 4 x 8 = 32, night food = 4 x 4 = 16, night drinks = 15 x 4 = 60; daily food = 96, daily drinks = 92, weekly food = 384, weekly drinks = 368. Thu–Sat (3 days): day food = 15 x 8 = 120, day drinks = 5 x 8 = 40, night food = 5 x 6 = 30, night drinks = 20 x 6 = 120; daily food = 150, daily drinks = 160, weekly food = 450, weekly drinks = 480. Totals: weekly food orders = 834, weekly drink orders = 848.

math.setup: Split by day group and day-part; multiply orders/hr x hours x days
steps: Sun–Wed day food: 10 x 8 hrs = 80 orders/day
Sun–Wed night food: 4 x 4 hrs = 16 orders/day
Sun–Wed daily food total: 96; x 4 days = 384 weekly
Sun–Wed day drinks: 4 x 8 = 32; night drinks: 15 x 4 = 60; daily = 92; x 4 days = 368 weekly
Thu–Sat day food: 15 x 8 = 120; night food: 5 x 6 = 30; daily = 150; x 3 days = 450 weekly
Thu–Sat day drinks: 5 x 8 = 40; night drinks: 20 x 6 = 120; daily = 160; x 3 days = 480 weekly

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly revenue, COGS, and gross profit for food and drinks
questions.guidance: Revenue = orders x price. COGS uses cost percentage (food COGS = 88%, drinks COGS = 50%). Candidate should produce a clean table.

math.setup: Weekly revenue = orders x price; COGS = revenue x cost %

questions.guidance: Calculate hours per staff type across both day groups, then multiply by wage rate.

math.setup: Total hours = (Sun–Wed hours) + (Thu–Sat hours) per staff type
steps: Kitchen: Sun–Wed = 4 days x 12 hrs (12pm–12am) = 48 hrs; Thu–Sat = 3 days x 14 hrs (12pm–2am) = 42 hrs; total = 90 hrs; cost = 4 people x $10 x 90 hrs = $3,600
Bar: same schedule 90 hrs; 1 person x $5 x 90 = $450
Wait staff: same schedule 90 hrs; 3 people x $5 x 90 = $1,350

questions.guidance: Weekly profit = Revenue - COGS - Labor - Lease. Convert monthly lease to weekly (divide by 4). Then annualize.

math.setup: Weekly profit = weekly revenue - weekly COGS - weekly labor - weekly lease

questions.prompt: Question 1: The client estimates startup capital of $500K. How long to break even, and what is the 5-year ROI? (Assume no interest.)
questions.guidance: Break-even = startup cost / annual profit. 5-year ROI = (annual profit x 5 - startup cost) / startup cost. Candidate should recognize the low return and contextualize vs. alternative investments.

steps: Annual ROI: 4.1% / 5 ≈ less than 1% per year

brainstorming.prompt: What additional revenue streams or cost-reduction strategies might improve the business case for the father?

categories.name: Additional revenue streams
ideas: Happy hour promotions to boost off-peak volume

categories.name: Cost reduction / capital efficiency
ideas: Purchase used equipment instead of new
Minimal interior redesign to reduce startup costs
Negotiate favorable lease terms or a shorter initial lease
Explore franchise or co-branding model to share startup costs

categories.name: Pricing and margin levers
ideas: Build brand loyalty to support premium pricing over time
Shift product mix toward higher-margin drinks

categories.name: Capacity and operating model
ideas: Optimize staffing to match demand (e.g., fewer kitchen staff on slow nights)
Extend hours on high-demand nights to capture more revenue
Consider kitchen-closed model on low-food-demand nights to cut COGS and labor

recommendation: From a financial perspective the sports bar is projected to be profitable at ~$104K annual profit, but the 4.8-year payback and <1% annual ROI on $500K startup capital are weak relative to other investment options
The father should benchmark this return against alternative investments (e.g., index funds, real estate) before committing; current projections do not strongly favor the sports bar
risks: Several costs are excluded from the model (utilities, marketing, licenses, insurance, equipment maintenance) — actual profit will be lower
Sudden rise in food COGS (supply shortage) or increase in minimum wages would compress already thin margins
Customer volume may decline after initial opening buzz — actual traffic could be lower than exhibit benchmarks
Location quality and competitive density are not factored in and could significantly affect foot traffic
next_steps: Incorporate all excluded costs (utilities, marketing, etc.) into the profitability model for a fully loaded view
Investigate ways to reduce startup capital requirements (used equipment, phased remodel) to shorten break-even
Explore additional revenue streams (events, advertising) to improve ROI
Have the father compare this opportunity against 2–3 alternative investments of similar size and horizon
